subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A chemical signal (ligand) produces a response only in specific target cells because those cells have:
questions.explain: Only cells with the matching receptor can bind the ligand and respond, giving signalling specificity.

questions.q: Steroid hormones can pass directly through the plasma membrane because they are:
questions.explain: Being lipophilic, steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors, often affecting gene expression.

questions.q: Peptide (protein) hormones such as insulin usually act by:
options: Binding surface receptors and triggering signal transduction inside the cell
questions.explain: Water-soluble hormones cannot cross the membrane, so they bind cell-surface receptors and set off intracellular cascades.

questions.q: A drug that binds a receptor and activates it, mimicking the natural ligand, is best described as an:
questions.explain: Agonists activate receptors; antagonists block them without activating.

questions.q: Signalling in which a secreted molecule affects nearby cells a short distance away is described as:
questions.explain: Paracrine signals act locally; endocrine signals travel in the blood to distant targets.

questions.q: The electrical charge difference across a neuron's membrane at rest is the:
questions.explain: The resting potential (about -70 mV) is maintained mainly by the sodium–potassium pump and ion permeabilities.

questions.q: Depolarisation during an action potential is caused mainly by:
options: Sodium ions rushing into the neuron
questions.explain: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ influx reverses the membrane potential.

questions.q: Repolarisation of the membrane after the peak of an action potential is due to:
options: Potassium ions moving out of the neuron
questions.explain: Voltage-gated potassium channels open and K+ efflux restores the negative internal charge.

questions.q: Myelination speeds up nerve impulses because the action potential:
options: Jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction)
Travels more slowly along the axon
questions.explain: In myelinated axons the impulse leaps from node to node, greatly increasing conduction speed.

questions.q: At a chemical synapse, the arrival of an action potential causes the release of neurotransmitter when:
options: Calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal and vesicles fuse with the membrane
The synapse depolarises the axon backward
questions.explain: Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis of neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.

questions.q: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the:
questions.explain: Binding to postsynaptic receptors opens ion channels and may trigger a new impulse in the next neuron.

questions.q: The action potential is described as 'all-or-nothing', meaning:
options: A stimulus at or above threshold produces a full-sized impulse; below threshold produces none
Its size varies with stimulus strength
questions.explain: Stimulus strength is coded by the frequency of impulses, not their size.

questions.q: Signal transduction refers to the process by which:
options: An external signal is converted into a response inside the cell
Nerve impulses travel down an axon
questions.explain: Binding of a ligand to a receptor triggers a cascade of intracellular events (e.g. second messengers) producing a response.

questions.q: Some pesticides and nerve agents block the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine. The likely effect at synapses is:
options: Continued stimulation of the postsynaptic neuron
questions.explain: If acetylcholine is not removed, receptors are repeatedly activated, causing overstimulation.

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose by binding target cells and causing them to:
options: Take up more glucose from the blood
questions.explain: Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, illustrating endocrine control of homeostasis.

questions.q: The sodium–potassium pump helps maintain the resting potential by moving:
options: Sodium out and potassium into the neuron using ATP
Sodium into and potassium out passively
questions.explain: The pump actively exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+, maintaining the ion gradients needed for the resting potential.

questions.q: During the refractory period a neuron cannot easily fire again, which ensures that impulses:
options: Travel in one direction and are discrete
questions.explain: The refractory period prevents backward propagation and sets a limit on impulse frequency.

questions.q: Compared with nerve signalling, hormonal (endocrine) signalling generally produces responses that are:
options: Slower in onset but longer lasting
questions.explain: Hormones travel in the blood, giving slower but more sustained, widespread effects than rapid neural signals.

questions.q: A neuron that carries impulses from receptors towards the central nervous system is a:
questions.explain: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses to the CNS; motor (efferent) neurons carry them to effectors.

questions.q: Because target-cell receptors are specific, a single hormone in the blood can:
options: Affect only cells possessing its receptor
Change the DNA sequence of all cells
questions.explain: Receptor specificity allows a bloodborne hormone to produce responses in only its target tissues.
